strong_form: A program that counts, in a news outlet's text, the relative use of emotively loaded versus neutral members of synonym sets (Russell conjugates, e.g. 'firm/obstinate/pig-headed') yields a slant score that correlates well with independent measures of slant (human-coded bias ratings, audience ideology, or partisan-phrase indices) without human reading of the articles.
weak_form: Word choice among near-synonyms carries a measurable slant signal that a lexicon can partly detect, useful as one input alongside validation.
refuted_if: A conjugate-lexicon score, applied to a large corpus of outlets, shows low agreement with human-coded slant or audience ideology, or results flip across reasonable lexicon choices, as has been found for off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries.

prior_art.citation: Future of Capitalism, quoting Eric Weinstein's post on Russell Conjugation proposing a crawler against a look-up table of conjugates
Gentzkow & Shapiro, 'What Drives Media Slant?' (NBER w12707 / Econometrica 2010): slant measured from frequencies of partisan phrases like 'death tax'
Boukes et al., 'What's the Tone? Easy Doesn't Do It': off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries show poor validity and little agreement on news
'Four best practices for measuring news sentiment using off-the-shelf dictionaries: a large-scale p-hacking experiment'

strongest_criticism: The data-driven version already exists and works (Gentzkow-Shapiro learn partisan phrases from Congress and validate against reader ideology), so the idea is not new; meanwhile the hand-built-lexicon version faces the documented failure of dictionary methods on news, where connotation depends on context, quotation, and audience, and scores vary wildly across lexicons. 'Without reading it' also hides that someone must read enough to build and validate the conjugate table, and outlets quoting opponents' loaded terms will be misscored.
